4 – 16 October 2026

Japan Central Alps
by Ninja Tours

Eleven riding days out of Tokyo, ~1,918 km (1,192 mi), ten onsen stays and one round of golf, for three riders — volcano roads, the Sea of Japan coast, and a hot spring every night.

Tokyo → Shima Onsen → Niigata (Sanjo) → Zao (Kaminoyama) → Nikaho Onsen → Iwate (Shizukuishi) → Naruko Onsen → Kaminoyama Onsen → Aizu (Higashiyama) → Yunishigawa Onsen → Tokyo

Sunday 10/4

Arrive Tokyo

On the road

Landed at Haneda Terminal 3 behind schedule. We came in on the minibus booked through Booking.com, US$66.96, door to door to the Asakusa View Hotel. The hotel sits on top of Tsukuba Express Asakusa station, one stop and about three minutes from Minami-Senju and Rushcorp.

Worth stopping for

  • Senso-ji and Nakamise-doriinfo — five minutes' walk from most Asakusa hotels, and best after dark when the day crowds have gone.
  • Kappabashi kitchenware streetinfo — a few hundred metres of chef's knives, cast iron and lacquerware, if we want something to ship home.
  • Hoppy-doriinfo — a lane of open-fronted izakaya behind Senso-ji, and the easiest first-night dinner in Asakusa.

Watch for

Sort our IDPs, licences and passports into one pocket tonight. Rushcorp will want all three in the morning.

Lodging

Asakusa View Hotel (浅草ビューホテル)

浅草 Asakusa is written 浅 (asa) shallow and 草 (kusa) grass. The hotel sits on top of Tsukuba Express Asakusa station — one stop and about three minutes from Minami-Senju, where we collect the bikes in the morning. Rated 4.1 across nearly 7,900 reviews, with upper floors looking over Senso-ji to the Skytree. The recurring complaint is noise, so ask for a high floor away from the street. Booked 4–5 October, two rooms, US$601, free cancellation.

www.viewhotels.jp/asakusa ↗

How to play a flyover

One file holds all ten riding days. Download it once and every flyover is in it — there is nothing to unpack and nothing to set up.

Download all ten flyovers one file · 1 MB ↓

  1. Click the green Download all ten flyovers button just above — or, for a single day, the Fly this day in Google Earth button at the top of any riding day. One click starts the download; the file lands in your Downloads folder.
  2. Double-click the downloaded file. Google Earth Pro opens and the days appear in the Places panel on the left, in date order. You need Earth Pro on a Mac or PC — the phone app and the browser version cannot play tours. It is free: download Google Earth Pro ↗ if it is not already installed.
  3. Turn the arrow down beside the day you want, so it points down instead of right. If all you can see is the trip name, turn its arrow down first and the ten days appear underneath.
  4. Click the little video-camera icon that appears. The flyover starts on its own and flies the whole day nose to tail.
  5. Click anywhere on the globe once it is running, and the blurry line across the view goes away. Playback controls sit at the bottom left if you want to pause or start again.

Two optional extras. Each riding day also has its own button further down, if you only want one. And if you would rather not open the file every time, drag the Japan 2026 · Tōhoku loop folder into My Places once and it stays there.

On the road

Pickup at Rushcorp, then north out of the city on Route 4 — over the Arakawa, west along the river, and out through Itabashi on surface roads rather than straight onto an expressway. A quiet first hour by Tokyo standards, which is the whole point on a morning when all three of us are still learning to keep left. Out into Gunma as far as Takasaki, then over Mount Haruna on prefectural Route 28. The climb from the Takasaki side narrows at Matsunozawa Pass — no room for anything large — then opens out at Lake Haruna, a caldera lake at 1,084 m (3,556 ft) with Haruna-Fuji standing over it, and runs down the far side two lanes wide with climbing lanes to Higashi-Agatsuma. From there west up the Agatsuma valley on R145 through Nakanojo, where a narrow road climbs the last few kilometres to Hinatami at the top of Shima Onsen, inside Joshin'etsu-kogen National Park. 179 km (111 mi) and about four hours in the saddle — and not the gentle first day it looks on paper, because Haruna is a real mountain road and it lands in the afternoon of the day we pick the bikes up.

Running order

Six hours for 179 km sounds generous. About four and a half of it is riding — the first 50 km are Tokyo traffic and the last 60 are mountain road — which leaves roughly ninety minutes of stopping on a day with jet lag, unfamiliar bikes and the wrong side of the road. That is two stops, not four.

10:00Leave Rushcorp. Don’t stop for the first 50 km — it is Route 4 and suburban arterials, nothing worth the time, and this is where we bank the buffer. Kawagoe’s kurazukuri street is genuinely lovely, but it is 3.8 km (2.4 mi) off the line and through town traffic: forty minutes round trip we will want later.
12:45–13:25Takasaki, 122 km (76 mi) in. Fuel and lunch. The one non-negotiable stop — last easy services before the climb, and we want full tanks before Route 28. Takasaki is the daruma town, and Shorinzan Daruma-ji is 3 km off if we are curious, but on a first day just eat and go.
14:25–14:50Lake Haruna, 145 km (90 mi) in. The payoff: a caldera lake at 1,084 m (3,556 ft) with Haruna-Fuji standing over it, the road running 300 m from the water. Mid-October should have colour coming in at that altitude.
15:10–15:20Nakanojo, 163 km (101 mi) in. Convenience store and the last fuel before the valley narrows.
15:30–15:40The Shima potholes, 168 km (104 mi) in. Eight water-bored shafts in the riverbed, free, a two-minute walk from the car park.
16:00Tsuruya, 11 km (7 mi) on from the potholes. Check-in runs 15:00 to 17:00, so this lands mid-window with an hour in hand.

Worth stopping for

  • Takasaki, the daruma towninfo — 122 km (76 mi) in. Shorinzan Daruma-ji started making them here in the 18th century as winter work for local farmers, and Takasaki still turns out most of Japan’s daruma. The round base is weighted, so a knocked-over daruma rights itself: 七転び八起き, fall down seven times, get up eight. The temple is 3 km (1.9 mi) off the line.
  • Mount Harunainfo — the reason Route 28 is on this route at all. A tight climb out of Takasaki, pinched at Matsunozawa Pass, then hairpins up to the caldera rim.
  • Lake Harunainfo — 145 km (90 mi) in, the caldera lake at 1,084 m (3,556 ft), with Haruna-Fuji standing 1,390 m (4,562 ft) over the far shore. The obvious place to stop before the run down to Agatsuma.
  • The Shima potholesinfo — 168 km (104 mi) in. 四万の甌穴群. Eight shafts bored straight down into the riverbed rock, not by the water but by pebbles caught in a standing eddy and turning in the same spot for centuries. The smallest is 20 cm across; the largest is over 3 m wide and 3.2 m deep. A Gunma natural monument since 1971. Right on R353 about ten kilometres short of the ryokan, free, with a car park and a two-minute walk down to the decks — and the same blue water as the lakes, held in rock cylinders.
  • Shima Blueinfo — Okushima Lake and Shima Lake hold an unusually vivid blue from suspended minerals. Best in flat morning light.
  • Sekizenkaninfo — the 1691 inn with the red bridge, five minutes down the valley from Tsuruya. Widely cited as an inspiration for the bathhouse in Spirited Away, though Ghibli has never confirmed any single model. The oldest surviving wooden onsen building in Japan either way.
  • Hinatami Yakushidoinfo — a 1598 temple hall built over the spring, one of the oldest surviving onsen structures in Japan and an Important Cultural Property. A few minutes' walk from the inn.

Watch for

Jet lag plus a mountain road on day one. Haruna comes late in the day, when we are tiring and least used to riding on the left, and the Takasaki-side hairpins are the narrow ones. Start early enough that the pass is done well before dusk.

Lodging

Shikanozoki-no-yu Tsuruya (鹿覗きの湯 つるや)

The name reads “Deer-Peeking Hot Spring” — 鹿覗きの湯, from deer that came down to the water. つるや is usually written 鶴屋: 鶴 (tsuru) crane, 屋 (ya) shop or house, so “Crane House” — a classic Japanese business name. Rated 4.1 from 280 reviews, at the quiet top end of the Shima valley. Four private baths plus rooms with their own tub — the large rock bath is what guests single out. English is spoken and reviewers repeatedly mention how well the staff handle foreign guests. A few note the price sits high for what the rooms are.

On the road

Back down the Shima valley to Nakanojo, then west through Kusatsu and up onto the Shiga-Kusatsu Kogen Route. R292 crosses the range at Shibu Pass, 2,172 m (7,126 ft) — the highest point of any national road in Japan — with Kusatsu-Shirane steaming beside it. Down the far side to Jigokudani and Shibu Onsen, then north through Iiyama, across the Chikuma into Niigata, and on through Tsunan and Tokamachi to the Uonuma plain and Sanjo. 242 km (150 mi) and about five and a half hours in the saddle: the longest day of the trip, and the best road on it.

Running order

The longest day of the trip and the one with no slack in it. 242 km, about five and a half hours riding, and Snow Peak stops taking check-ins at 16:30 — so the stops stay short. Coffee and a sandwich at a 7-Eleven rather than a sit-down lunch.

09:00Leave Tsuruya, down the Shima valley to Nakanojo, then west.
10:15–10:40Kusatsu, 43 km (27 mi) in. Fuel, then the Yubatake — it is a five-minute walk each way from the car park, so the look itself is about ten minutes. Last easy petrol before the pass.
11:35–11:50Shibu Pass, 71 km (44 mi) in, 2,172 m (7,126 ft). Fifteen minutes at the highest point of any national road in Japan.
12:15–13:00Jigokudani, 82 km (51 mi) in. Forty-five minutes. Pay the ¥500 (about US$3) for the upper car park — 10 to 15 minutes’ walk each way, against roughly thirty from the free Kanbayashi lot. The park runs 8:30 to 17:00 in October, ¥800 (about US$5) to enter. Expect macaques but not the winter photograph: in warm months the wardens have to coax them into the bath.
14:45–14:50Tokamachi, 166 km (103 mi) in. Fuel.
16:15Snow Peak, 76 km (47 mi) on from Tokamachi. Check-in closes at 16:30, so every minute over at Jigokudani comes straight out of this.

Worth stopping for

  • The Yubatake, Kusatsuinfo — 43 km (27 mi) in. 湯畑 reads “hot water field,” and it is a cooling plant in the middle of the street. Four thousand litres a minute arrive at 55 °C, too hot to bathe in. Kusatsu will not thin its water with cold — at pH 2.1 the strength is the whole point — so instead the flow is spread across seven open wooden troughs and cooled by air alone before it drops to the pool and runs on to the bathhouses. The sulphur that settles in the troughs is scraped out, dried and sold as yunohana (湯の花, “hot water flower” — the mineral crust the spring leaves behind, packaged as a bath additive so you can make onsen water at home). The granite surround was going to be rectangular until Okamoto Taro — the artist behind the Tower of the Sun at Expo ’70 — was asked to design it in 1975 and made it a gourd instead, so that an organic outline would play against the straight lines of the troughs inside. He laid out the promenade that circles it too, and his name is cut into the stone. Parking: Kusatsu Parking is ¥100 per 30 minutes and about 40 spaces; the larger Yubatake Kanko Parking has a motorcycle area but charges a flat two-hour minimum. Both are about five minutes’ walk, so a ten-minute look costs nearer twenty-five door to door.
  • Shibu Passinfo — 71 km (44 mi) in, the highest point of any national road in Japan, 2,172 m (7,126 ft) on R292, marked by a stone and a signboard, and usually a row of bikes parked in front of both. The wording matters: this is the highest national road. Japan’s highest paved road is the Norikura Skyline at 2,702 m (8,865 ft), but it has been closed to private vehicles since 2003 — buses, taxis and bicycles only — so 2,172 m is as high as we can ride.
  • Jigokudani Monkey Parkinfo — 82 km (51 mi) in, wild macaques at a hot-spring pool in the valley below Shiga Kōgen. Admission ¥800 (about US$5) each. Park free at Kanbayashi and walk the 2 km (1.2 mi) Yumichi trail, about 30 minutes, or pay ¥500 (about US$3) at the Jigokudani lot for a 15-minute walk up a narrow logging road.
  • Shibu Onseninfo — nine public baths along a stone lane, five minutes from the monkey park and the traditional pairing with it.
  • The Uonuma rice fieldsinfo — harvested and gold in October, and the source of the rice we will be eating all week.
  • Tsubame-Sanjoinfo — Japan's metalworking capital. Knife and tool workshops open to visitors, and the reason Snow Peak is headquartered here.

Watch for

R292 over Shibu Pass runs roughly May to late November, so early October is comfortably inside the season — but not far from the end of it. The stretch past Kusatsu-Shirane is an active volcano and has carried gas-zone no-stopping rules and gate hours that change from year to year, so check the Shiga Kogen traffic page the evening before, or call the Gunma prefecture road office in Nakanojo on 0279-75-3047 — Nakanojo is the town we ride out of that morning. The fallback is the original line: north to Minakami and over Mikuni Pass on R17, about 215 km (134 mi) and an easier day, but nothing like the road.

Lodging

Snow Peak FIELD SUITE SPA HEADQUARTERS (スノーピーク)

Snow Peak writes its name in katakana, スノーピーク, so there is no kanji reading. The town, 三条 Sanjo, is 三 (san) three and 条 (jo) line. Rated 4.4 from over 500 reviews — not a ryokan but a design resort on Snow Peak's own campfield. Architect-built suites and standalone cabins with decks, plus indoor and outdoor onsen and a sauna looking at the mountains. Reviewers rate the spa and the food highly and describe the site as exceptionally quiet at night. Tattoos are allowed in the baths only during limited hours, so confirm at check-in.

On the road

North across the Niigata plain to Shibata, then R113 east up the Arakawa valley — the old Yonezawa highway, a river road nearly the whole way — over the prefectural border at Oguni and through Nan'yo to Kaminoyama.

Running order

181 km and about four hours riding — the first day of the trip with real slack in it. Snow Peak checks out at 11:00, Koyo takes check-ins until 17:00 and dinner is from 18:30, so nothing is pushing.

10:00Leave Snow Peak. Check-out is 11:00, so there is no need to hurry over breakfast. North across the Niigata plain.
11:20–11:30Shibata, 65 km (40 mi) in. Fuel.
12:10–13:00Michi-no-eki Sekikawa, 96 km (60 mi) in. Lunch where R113 runs through the Arakawa gorge — the prettiest stretch of the day.
13:30–13:45Oguni, 117 km (73 mi) in. Beech forest either side of the road, which should be turning at this altitude.
15:10–15:40Kaminoyama Castle, 181 km (112 mi) in. The castle and the samurai street below it, 700 m short of the ryokan — easier now than doubling back tomorrow.
15:45Koyo, 700 m (0.4 mi) on from the castle. Check-in runs to 17:00 and dinner is from 18:30, so there is a bath and an hour spare before either.

Worth stopping for

  • Michi-no-eki Sekikawa and the Arakawa gorgeinfo — 96 km (60 mi) in, the prettiest stretch of R113 and a natural lunch stop.
  • Oguniinfo — 117 km (73 mi) in, beech forest either side of the road, which should be turning at this altitude in early October.
  • Kaminoyama Castleinfo — 181 km (112 mi) in, the castle and the samurai residences below it; free foot baths are dotted through the town.

Lodging

Nihon-no-yado Koyo (日本の宿 古窯)

日本の宿 means simply “inn of Japan.” 古窯 Koyo is 古 (ko) old and 窯 (yo) kiln — an old pottery kiln on the site gave the inn its name. Rated 4.4 from over 2,200 reviews, which is a very large sample for a ryokan. Rooftop bath with an outdoor section, some rooms with private open-air tubs, and dinners built around Yonezawa beef and Tsuyahime rice. Breakfast is served in a large hall, which a few reviewers find impersonal for the price.

On the road

North past Yamagata city to Sagae, then R112 west over the Gassan range — the road threads between Gassan and Yudono-san, and the tunnels and snowsheds along it are there for a reason. Down onto the Shonai plain at Tsuruoka and Sakata, then R7 up the coast to Fukura, where the Chokai Blue Line turns inland and climbs to about 1,100 m (3,600 ft) on the flank of Mt. Chokai before dropping back to the sea at Kisakata. 206 km (128 mi), and the best of it is in the last fifty.

Running order

206 km and about four and a half hours riding. Koyo checks out at 10:00 and Ichie takes check-ins from 15:00 to 17:00. Leaving at 09:00 rather than at check-out matters because the Blue Line sits at the very end of the day: the early start puts an hour between anything that goes wrong in the morning and the one road we came for, and leaves that hour spare on the mountain if it doesn’t.

09:00Leave Koyo. North past Yamagata to Sagae, then west onto R112.
10:00–10:15Michi-no-eki Nishikawa, 45 km (28 mi) in. Coffee at the foot of Gassan.
11:30–12:15Tsuruoka, 113 km (70 mi) in. Lunch.
12:40–13:00Sakata, 136 km (85 mi) in. The Sankyo rice warehouses and their row of zelkova.
13:25Fukura, 155 km (96 mi) in. The Blue Line starts here.
14:05–14:25Ohira, 175 km (109 mi) in. The top of the Blue Line, about 1,100 m (3,600 ft). Twenty minutes is the plan — but the 09:00 start means we can take an hour here if the weather is worth it, and still be at Ichie inside the window.
15:00–15:15Kisakata, 194 km (121 mi) in. The islands stranded in the rice paddies.
15:35Ichie, 12 km (7 mi) on from Kisakata. Check-in opens at 15:00, so this arrives right on time.

Worth stopping for

  • Yamadera (Risshaku-ji)info — a thousand stone steps up a cliff to a temple among the rocks, where Basho wrote the cicada haiku. 10.9 km (6.8 mi) off the line, so allow ninety minutes all in — which does not fit alongside the Blue Line on the same day.
  • Sakatainfo — 136 km (85 mi) in, the Sankyo rice warehouses with their row of zelkova trees, and the Homma Museum garden.
  • The Chokai Blue Lineinfo — starts 155 km (96 mi) in: prefectural route 210, 39 km (24 mi) from Fukura up to about 1,100 m (3,600 ft) at Ohira and back down to Kisakata, sea to summit to sea. The gates shut at night from around 24 October and the road closes for winter in early November, so 8 October is comfortably clear of both — but the dates move each year.
  • Kisakatainfo — 194 km (121 mi) in. 九十九島, the ninety-nine islands, and the strangest landscape on the route. About 2,500 years ago a flank of Mount Chokai collapsed and ran out to the sea as a debris avalanche; water filled the hollows between the rubble mounds and left a shallow lagoon studded with wooded islets. It became one of the most admired views in the north — Basho came in 1689 and set it against Matsushima, the one cheerful and this one melancholy. Then on 10 July 1804 a magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck directly beneath it. Three to five hundred people died, a one-metre tsunami flooded three hundred houses here and in Sakata, and the seabed was lifted clear of the water. The lagoon drained. Farmers turned the new ground into rice fields and left the islands standing, so what we ride past is a flat plain of paddy with the old islets marooned in it as tree-covered mounds, Chokai filling the sky behind. A National Natural Monument since 1934. The mirror reflections people photograph come in May and June when the fields are flooded; on 8 October it will be cut stubble.

Watch for

Kisakata is known for rock oysters — worth asking the inn whether they are still in season.

Lodging

Ichie (一会)

一会 Ichie is 一 (ichi) one and 会 (e) meeting, from 一期一会 — “one lifetime, one encounter,” the tea-ceremony idea that every meeting happens only once. Rated 3.7 from 250 reviews — the lowest-rated stop on the trip, and worth knowing before we arrive. The rooms were renovated a few years ago and reviewers praise the cypress open-air baths and the traditional breakfast; some rooms have a private sauna and cold plunge. The complaints are consistent too: an ageing building and inconsistent front-desk service.

On the road

Inland from Kisakata across the Akita rice plain to Daisen, then north to Kakunodate — the samurai quarter, black wooden fences and weeping cherries along them. On past Lake Tazawa, the deepest lake in Japan, and over Sengan Pass on R46 into Iwate, finishing under Mt. Iwate at Shizukuishi. 156 km (97 mi) and the shortest riding day of the trip — the Chokai Blue Line is behind us, ridden yesterday afternoon.

Running order

156 km and about three and a quarter hours riding — the shortest riding day of the trip. Ichie checks out at 10:00, Mori-no-kaze takes check-ins until 17:00, and dinner is not until 19:30. Nothing about this day is tight, which after yesterday’s Blue Line finish is the point.

10:00Leave Ichie. Inland from Kisakata across the Akita plain.
11:50–12:50Kakunodate, 86 km (53 mi) in. The samurai quarter and lunch — an hour is about right to walk the black-fenced street.
13:20–13:50Lake Tazawa, 108 km (67 mi) in. Japan’s deepest lake, 2.6 km (1.6 mi) off the line.
14:25–14:55Nyuto Onsen, 120 km (75 mi) in. Optional — 7.8 km (4.8 mi) off the line up a dead-end valley. Worth it only if we want to see it; the baths are for staying guests.
15:30–15:40Sengan Pass, 138 km (86 mi) in. The R46 crossing into Iwate.
16:05Hotel Mori-no-kaze Oshuku, 18 km (11 mi) on from Sengan Pass.

Worth stopping for

  • Kakunodateinfo — 86 km (53 mi) in, the best-preserved samurai district in the north, dark wooden walls and weeping cherries. Twenty minutes' walk end to end.
  • Lake Tazawainfo — 108 km (67 mi) in, the deepest lake in Japan at 423 m (1,388 ft), and a startling cobalt blue. The gilded Tatsuko statue stands in the shallows on the west shore.
  • Nyuto Onseninfo — 120 km (75 mi) in, up a side road from Tazawa; if we have a spare hour, Tsurunoyu's milky open-air bath is the famous one.
  • Sengan Passinfo — the R46 crossing into Iwate at 138 km (86 mi) in, 1.3 km (0.8 mi) off the line. Tunnels and long sweepers rather than hairpins.

Watch for

The Chokai Blue Line is seasonal and closes for winter. Mid-October should be fine, but confirm before committing to it as our route.

Lodging

Hotel Mori-no-kaze Oshuku (ホテル森の風鶯宿)

森の風 is 森 (mori) forest and 風 (kaze) wind — “wind in the forest.” 鶯宿 Oshuku is 鶯 (uguisu) bush warbler and 宿 (shuku) lodging: a warbler is said to have healed itself in the spring here. Rated 4.2 from over 300 reviews, at Oshuku Onsen in Shizukuishi with Mt. Iwate behind it. Three linked buildings, large rooms, and options with a private in-room onsen. Reviewers say the exterior looks dated but the interiors are well kept, and single out the dining hall and the evening performance. Two minutes from the golf course.

Sunday 10/11

Iwate (Shizukuishi) → Naruko Onsen

Iwate (Shizukuishi)175 km (108 mi)Naruko Onsen

On the road

South out of Shizukuishi down the west side of the Ou range — not the R4 corridor through Morioka but the quieter line through Nishiwaga and the Yokote basin, forest and reservoirs most of the way. Into Miyagi past Onikobe, and the last stretch drops through the Naruko Gorge, which in mid-October is one of the best foliage runs in Tohoku. 175 km (108 mi): a transit day with a very good ending.

Running order

175 km and about three and three quarter hours riding. The thing to know is that Naruko Hotel stops taking check-ins at 16:00, an hour earlier than most of the trip. The gorge is the last three kilometres of the day, so we can stop there and still be in on time — but there is no room for a long lunch as well.

10:00Leave Mori-no-kaze. South down the west side of the Ou range.
11:10–11:20Nishiwaga, 51 km (32 mi) in. Fuel. Reservoir country with almost nothing on the road.
11:50–12:40Yokote, 73 km (45 mi) in. Lunch — Yokote yakisoba if we want the local thing.
14:15–14:35Onikobe, 144 km (89 mi) in. Steam vents and small onsen, about 4.7 km (2.9 mi) off the line.
15:15–15:30Naruko Gorge, 172 km (107 mi) in. Peak colour in mid-October.
15:35Naruko Hotel, 3 km (2 mi) on from the gorge — check-in closes at 16:00.

Worth stopping for

  • Nishiwagainfo — 51 km (32 mi) in and 1.9 km (1.2 mi) off the line. Reservoir country, almost no traffic, and the snowiest inhabited place in Honshu in winter.
  • The Yokote basininfo — 73 km (45 mi) in, 1.9 km (1.2 mi) off. Rice plain ringed by mountains; Yokote yakisoba is the local lunch if the timing lands.
  • Onikobeinfo — 144 km (89 mi) in, about 4.7 km (2.9 mi) off. A geothermal basin of steam vents and small onsen just before the drop into Naruko.
  • Naruko Gorgeinfo — 172 km (107 mi) in, the Ofukazawa bridge viewpoint is the classic shot. Naruko town is also the home of kokeshi dolls, with workshops open to visitors.

Watch for

Naruko Gorge at peak colour on the Sunday of a long weekend will be busy. Ride it early or late, and expect the gorge car parks to be full in the middle of the day.

Lodging

Naruko Hotel (鳴子ホテル)

鳴子 Naruko is 鳴 (naru) to cry out and 子 (ko) child — from a legend of an infant who cried at the spring. Rated 4.2 from nearly 1,700 reviews, operating since 1873 and five minutes from the station. Water is drawn from several sources and is often milky white — the colour shifts day to day. Private baths can be booked for about ¥2,000 (about US$13) for fifty minutes, the yukata are printed with kokeshi (こけし — the limbless wooden dolls Naruko is famous for), and the dinner buffet gets consistently good marks. The whole town smells of sulphur.

Naruko Onsen → Kaminoyama Onsen

On the road

West from Naruko to Ginzan Onsen, then south and east across to Akiu on the edge of Sendai before turning back west over the Zao Echo Line — over the shoulder of Zao, past the Okama crater lake — and down to Kaminoyama. 196 km (122 mi): a long way round, and the Echo Line is the reason.

Running order

196 km and about four and a quarter hours riding, and Hashimotoya also closes check-in at 16:00. Leaving at Naruko’s 10:00 check-out leaves under two hours of stopping for a day that has Ginzan Onsen and the Zao Echo Line in it, so 09:00 is the departure that works.

09:00Leave Naruko Hotel. West towards Ginzan.
10:00–10:45Ginzan Onsen, 42 km (26 mi) in. Park outside the village — the street itself is closed to cars.
12:20–13:00Akiu Onsen, 119 km (74 mi) in. Lunch on the edge of Sendai.
14:10–14:35The Okama crater, 165 km (103 mi) in, on the Zao Echo Line. 2.0 km (1.2 mi) off the line.
15:20Hatago-no-kokoro Hashimotoya, 31 km (19 mi) on from the Okama — check-in closes at 16:00.

Worth stopping for

  • Ginzan Onseninfo — 42 km (26 mi) in, a short detour north of Obanazawa; Taisho-era wooden inns facing each other across a stream, gas lamps at dusk. The most photographed hot spring street in Japan, and it earns it.
  • Akiu Onseninfo — 119 km (74 mi) in and 1.3 km (0.8 mi) off the line. Sendai’s own hot spring town, with the Akiu Otaki waterfall just upstream.
  • The Zao Echo Line and the Okama craterinfo — 165 km (103 mi) in, 2.0 km (1.2 mi) off. The crossing of the Zao range, with the Okama crater lake on the shoulder. It closes at night from early November and for winter shortly after, so early October is clear — but check before the day.
  • Kaminoyama Castleinfo — and the town's foot baths, this time with an afternoon to use them.

Watch for

Holiday Monday is the national return day, so expressways toward Tokyo will be solid. We are travelling the other way on back roads — no problem, but do not be tempted onto anything heading south.

Lodging

Hatago-no-kokoro Hashimotoya (旅籠の心 橋本屋)

旅籠 hatago was the word for an Edo-period travellers’ inn, and 心 (kokoro) is heart or spirit — “the spirit of the old inn.” 橋本屋 Hashimotoya is 橋 (hashi) bridge, 本 (moto) origin, 屋 (ya) house. Rated 4.5 from 338 reviews — the highest-rated stop on the trip, and a few doors from where we stayed on Day 3. A rabbit motif runs through the whole building down to the tableware, meals are served in private rooms, and both public baths have open-air sections. Reviewers describe the layout as a small maze and the presentation as the reason to come.

On the road

South from Kaminoyama through the Yonezawa basin and over into Fukushima, then up onto the Bandai-Azuma Lake Line, the southern of the two Bandai skyline roads, past Goshiki-numa and its five-coloured ponds. Down to Inawashiro and west to Aizuwakamatsu. 158 km (98 mi).

Running order

158 km and about three and a quarter hours riding, with check-in open until 17:00. An easy day, and the one where Yonezawa finally makes sense: it sits 0.9 km off this line, against 12.5 km on the 7th.

10:00Leave Hashimotoya. South through the Yonezawa basin.
10:45–11:15Yonezawa, 32 km (20 mi) in. The beef at source, and Uesugi Shrine if we want it — 0.9 km off the line.
12:40–13:20Tsuchiyu, about 95 km (59 mi) in. Lunch before the climb.
13:55–14:25Goshiki-numa, 120 km (75 mi) in, at the far end of the Bandai-Azuma Lake Line. The ponds are a short walk from the road.
15:10–15:45Tsuruga Castle, 155 km (96 mi) in, on the way into Aizuwakamatsu.
15:50Konjakutei, 3 km (2 mi) on from Tsuruga Castle.

Worth stopping for

  • The Bandai-Azuma Lake Lineinfo — 115 km (71 mi) in and 1.5 km (0.9 mi) off the line. A ridge road above Lake Akimoto and Lake Onogawa; the higher Skyline is a separate road and is not on this route.
  • Goshiki-numainfo — 120 km (75 mi) in, the five coloured ponds on the Ura-Bandai side, each a different shade from mineral content. A flat 3.6 km (2.2 mi) trail links them.
  • Lake Inawashiroinfo — the fourth largest in Japan, with Mt. Bandai reflected in it on a still morning.
  • Tsuruga Castleinfo — 155 km (96 mi) in, at Aizuwakamatsu, ten minutes from the inn.

Watch for

The Skyline has a seasonal night closure and volcanic gas restrictions near Jododaira. If it is shut, R13 south to R121 through Kitakata is the fallback and cuts the day to about 160 km (99 mi).

Lodging

Konjakutei (今昔亭)

今昔亭 Konjakutei is 今 (kon) now, 昔 (jaku) long ago, 亭 (tei) pavilion — “the pavilion of then and now.” Rated 4.3 from 252 reviews, at Higashiyama Onsen on the edge of Aizuwakamatsu. A small property where the service and the food are what reviewers write about — several mention the kitchen accommodating dietary requests without fuss. The baths here are indoor and modest, but guests can walk 150 m (492 ft) to the sister ryokan Harataki for an open-air bath facing the waterfall.

Aizu (Higashiyama) → Yunishigawa Onsen

Aizu (Higashiyama)188 km (117 mi)Yunishigawa Onsen

On the road

South-east out of Aizu towards Shirakawa, then west into Nasu — the Yumoto onsen village under Nasu-dake — and on to Shiobara, a gorge of hot springs and suspension bridges. West again past Kawaji and up the dead-end valley to Yunishigawa, where the road stops. 188 km (117 mi).

Running order

188 km and about four hours riding, squeezed by two things at once: Kamenoi closes check-in at 16:00 and the buffet starts around 17:30. Konjakutei’s 11:00 check-out is generous but leaving at it does not work — 10:00 does. Shirakawa Komine Castle is 6.4 km off the line and only fits with an earlier start than this.

10:00Leave Konjakutei. South-east out of Aizu.
11:55–12:40Nasu Yumoto, 93 km (58 mi) in. Lunch under Nasu-dake, 3.4 km (2.1 mi) off the line.
13:30–13:55Shiobara Onsen, 131 km (81 mi) in. The gorge and the suspension bridge, 0.3 km off the line.
14:45–14:55Kawaji Onsen, 169 km (105 mi) in. The turn up the Yunishigawa valley is here.
15:25Kamenoi Hotel, 19 km (12 mi) on from Kawaji — check-in closes at 16:00, dinner from about 17:30.

Worth stopping for

  • Shirakawa Komine Castleinfo — 66 km (41 mi) in, 6.4 km (4.0 mi) off the line. Rebuilt in timber to the original method, which is rare.
  • Nasu Kogen and Yumotoinfo — 93 km (58 mi) in, about 3.4 km (2.1 mi) off. Sulphur springs directly under Nasu-dake, and the imperial family’s summer villa country.
  • Shiobara Onsen and the Momiji Valley bridgeinfo — 131 km (81 mi) in and 0.3 km off the line. Eleven hot spring hamlets strung along a gorge, with a 320 m suspension footbridge over it.
  • Kawaji Onseninfo — 169 km (105 mi) in, 2.0 km (1.2 mi) off, where the Kinugawa and Male rivers meet. The turn up the Yunishigawa valley is here.
  • Yunishigawa villageinfo — founded by Heike refugees hiding after Dan-no-ura. Households here still avoid carp streamers and crowing roosters, on the grounds that either might have given the fugitives away.

Watch for

There is very little in the valley beyond the hotels, so dinner is wherever we are staying. Fill up in Kawaji rather than assuming we will find fuel further in.

Sika deer through the forest at both ends of this day — out of Aizu in the morning, and along the Nasu–Shiobara stretch in the afternoon. Both are thick with them, and October is the rut, when the animals move most. Our timings keep us off the road at dawn and dusk, which is when it actually bites, but if the day slips late, ease off through the trees: deer travel in groups, so one crossing in front of us means more are still to come.

Lodging

Kamenoi Hotel Nikko Yunishigawa (亀の井ホテル 日光湯西川)

亀の井 Kamenoi is 亀 (kame) tortoise and 井 (i) well. 湯西川 Yunishigawa is 湯 (yu) hot water, 西 (nishi) west, 川 (kawa) river; 日光 Nikko is 日 (ni) sun and 光 (ko) light. Rated 3.7 from 544 reviews, and the reviews split cleanly. It runs all-inclusive — drinks from 2pm, snacks from 4pm, late-night noodles — and reviewers consistently praise the food, the onsen and the setting. They just as consistently flag that the guest rooms are dated: this was the Heike Honjin before Kamenoi took it over, and the refurbishment reached the public areas more than the bedrooms.

Thursday 10/15

Yunishigawa Onsen → Tokyo

Yunishigawa Onsen237 km (147 mi)Tokyo

On the road

North-west first, up through Kawamata and into Okunikko — Yumoto Onsen, the Senjogahara marsh, Lake Chuzenji and Kegon Falls — then down the Irohazaka hairpins past Toshogu to Imaichi. South from there through Utsunomiya and on into Tokyo. 237 km (147 mi), and the first third of it is the best riding of the last week. It ends with city traffic and a handover, so build in margin.

Running order

237 km and about five hours riding, the second longest day of the trip, and it ends with a bike handover and Tokyo traffic rather than a hotel car park. Dinner at the sushi counter is 19:00. A 09:00 start gets the whole of Okunikko done properly and still has us at Rushcorp with the afternoon in hand.

09:00Leave Kamenoi. North-west up the valley.
10:00–10:15Kawamata, 40 km (25 mi) in. Last quiet stop before the climb into Okunikko.
11:00–11:30Senjogahara and Yumoto Onsen, 65 km (40 mi) in. Marsh plateau at about 1,400 m (4,600 ft).
11:45–12:05Lake Chuzenji and Kegon Falls, 72 km (45 mi) in.
12:20The Irohazaka, 80 km (50 mi) in. Forty-eight hairpins, one-way downhill. Ride it, do not stop on it.
12:30–13:15Nikko Toshogu, 86 km (53 mi) in.
16:05Rushcorp, 237 km (147 mi) — 151 km (94 mi) of it on from Toshogu, the longest unbroken run of the trip. Confirm the handover cut-off with Ninja Tours — it is the one time today nobody has told us.

Worth stopping for

  • Okunikko: Yumoto and Senjogaharainfo — 65 km (40 mi) in and under 2 km off the line. A high marsh plateau at about 1,400 m (4,600 ft) with Yumoto Onsen at the top of it.
  • Lake Chuzenji and Kegon Fallsinfo — 72 km (45 mi) in, 0.1 km off. A 97 m (318 ft) fall out of the lake, formed when Nantai dammed the valley.
  • The Irohazakainfo — 80 km (50 mi) in and on the line. Forty-eight hairpins down from Chuzenji, one-way downhill, each corner lettered for a syllable of the old Japanese alphabet. Peak colour in mid-October, which also means traffic.
  • Nikko Toshoguinfo — 86 km (53 mi) in, with the Shinkyo bridge too if we swing west before turning south. Adds about two hours.
  • Utsunomiya for gyozainfo — the city is famous for it and it is right on the route.

Watch for

Leave a buffer before the Rushcorp handover. City riding at the end of a long trip is where mistakes happen.

Macaques through Okunikko and on the Irohazaka. Troops sit in the road and around the car parks at Yumoto, Chuzenji and Kegon, and years of people feeding them from car windows have made them bold rather than shy. Do not eat in the open there, keep the panniers shut, and do not stop on the hairpins for one — a monkey on the Irohazaka is a reason to keep rolling, not to reach for a camera.

Dinner

鮨 明 高勢 (Sushi Aki Takase)

Rodger and Teruyo's favourite place for many decades — which is reason enough to make it the last dinner of the trip. A sushi counter in Negishi, one stop up the Hibiya Line from where we hand the bikes back. 鮨 is the older character for sushi, and a shop that chooses it over 寿司 is usually signalling a proper counter rather than a casual place. 明 (Aki) is the chef's given name and 高勢 (Takase) the family shop — the noren reads as two names, not one word.

It also turns a hundred this year. 高勢 opened on this ground in 1926, named for its founder 高橋勢太郎 Takahashi Setarō — 高 from Takahashi, 勢 from Setarō. It became an establishment haunt in the bubble years and then lost everything, and the craft moved to Asakusa under Aki's father, 高橋政嗣 Takahashi Masaji. In 2010 Aki — who trained in Western kitchens rather than sushi, at 小川軒 in Ochanomizu — reopened on the original Negishi site as a wa-bistro. When his father closed the Asakusa shop in 2012 it took the full name 鮨 明 高勢, and Masaji came to work alongside his son. So the counter stands at the family's first address, occupied again after eighty years away, and the 明 on the curtain is the chef's own given name. Whether that makes him the third or fourth generation depends on which account you read.

Lodging

Asakusa View Hotel Annex Rokku (浅草ビューホテル アネックス六区)

Back in Asakusa for the last night all together, but in Rokku — the old entertainment quarter west of Senso-ji, with Hanayashiki directly in front of the door and the temple four minutes away on foot. It opened in March 2023, so everything in it is new, and the rooms have the tub and shower separated rather than the usual moulded business-hotel unit. The tenth-floor Premium Lounge FURUMAI is free to every guest from 15:00 to 22:00, with Asakusa confections and coffee and a view of the Skytree and Senso-ji’s pagoda; it is built to look like a Showa-era cinema, which is what stood on this ground. One stop from Minami-Senju on the Tsukuba Express and two minutes’ walk, so the bike handover and our beds stay close together — and dinner in Negishi is under ten minutes by taxi.

Friday 10/16

Two-up pair departs · HND 16:05

On the road

Aim to be at Haneda Terminal 3 by about 13:00 for an international departure. Check out at 11:00, then about ten minutes on foot to Asakusa station, where the Toei Asakusa line runs through onto the Keikyu airport line — direct to Terminal 3 in roughly fifty minutes, no changes. Leaving by about 11:45 is comfortable. All three of us can ride that same train out of Asakusa: the two-up pair carry on to the airport, the solo rider gets off at Higashi-Ginza about fifteen minutes down the line. The alternative is the airport limousine from the main Asakusa View Hotel, five minutes away — it takes the bags off our hands, though traffic makes it less predictable. Worth having Ninja Tours confirm the outbound times.

Worth stopping for

  • Nakamise-doriinfo — open early, and a last chance for senbei and small gifts before the train. Four minutes’ walk from the hotel.
  • Nihombashi Mitsukoshiinfo — the depachika is the best food-gift hall in Tokyo, ten minutes straight down the Ginza line from Asakusa. Check what US customs allows before buying anything fresh.

Watch for

The solo rider stays on another night and moves hotels, Asakusa to Ginza. Confirm with Ninja Tours whether that night is covered or needs booking separately, and drop the bags at the Ginza hotel before heading back out.

Lodging

Millennium Mitsui Garden Hotel Tokyo (ミレニアム三井ガーデンホテル東京) — extra night for the solo rider

A move across town rather than an extension, and worth the bother for the last morning. The hotel is one minute from Higashi-Ginza Exit A1, which sits on the Toei Asakusa line — the same line out of Asakusa, so it is a direct ride with no changes. It also makes this the shortest airport run of anywhere on the trip: the hotel puts Haneda at about thirty minutes on the Keikyu Airport Rapid Express. Ginza station is two minutes the other way, Ginza Mitsukoshi two minutes from Higashi-Ginza through an underground passage, and Tsukiji Outer Market about ten minutes on foot — which is the one thing in Tokyo genuinely worth being up early for. No large public bath, which is what it gives up.

On the road

A late flight, so the whole day is usable. Check out at 12:00 and leave the bags with the front desk. Be at Haneda by about 17:15 — and from Higashi-Ginza, one minute from the door, that is a direct thirty-minute run on the Toei Asakusa line, so leaving around 16:30 is unhurried.

  • Senso-jiinfo — quiet before nine in the morning, which is the only time it ever is. About fifteen minutes back up the Toei Asakusa line.
  • Kappabashi kitchenware streetinfo — a few minutes past Senso-ji, and the right place to spend a final morning if we want a knife to take home.
  • Nihombashi Mitsukoshiinfo — if the shopping did not happen yesterday, fifteen minutes up the Toei Asakusa line. Ginza Mitsukoshi is three minutes from the door instead, most of it underground.
  • Tsukiji Outer Marketinfo — about ten minutes on foot, running roughly 05:00 to 14:00 with the sushi counters open from seven. The best breakfast in Tokyo and the only thing here worth setting an alarm for. Closed Sundays and national holidays, and some shops on Wednesdays — 10/17 is a Saturday, so it is open.

Watch for

Four and a half hours between checkout and the train. Leaving the bags at the hotel is easier than dragging them to the airport early.
